claim: RPD is the default mode of experienced decision makers in time-pressured field settings: they generate one plausible option, simulate it, and move on only if it fails. The 80-90 percent figure is secondary only (1986 study, 26 commanders / 156 decisions not verified); the naval study reports 95 percent recognitional. Gap search could not open the 1986 report (DTIC file damaged, 403); counts remain unverified.
agent_test: Compare single-first-candidate-then-test vs 4 parallel candidates at equal tokens on checkable tasks.

claim: Recognition-style intuition is only reliable where the environment has valid learnable cues and the expert had enough practice; confidence is not a valid signal of that.
schema_part: G10/S2 mode choice (route to direct only where cheap checks exist)
agent_test: Route by domain-validity label; compare calibration of agent confidence in high-validity vs low-validity task sets.
audit_note: Both sources include Gary Klein (a04/a05 are one paper), though Kahneman co-author makes the view cross-school; claim wording matches both.

claim: Informal expert judgment is noisy; simple consistent models beat the judges they model (Goldberg: 29 clinicians, 861 cases, 11 scales; Karelaia and Hogarth 2008 meta-analysis).
agent_test: Compare one sampled answer vs majority of 3-5 short independent samples at equal tokens.

claim: Prompting an LLM with an RPD-style recognise-then-simulate strategy raised care-seeking triage accuracy: 63.3 percent default to 67.6 percent RPD (13,500 answers, 10 models, 45 vignettes; OR 2.26). A data-frame prompt gave 66.7 percent. Single study; b01-b03 and c01-c07 are the same paper. Preprint numbers differed (RPD 70.2, default 64.7).
agent_test: Replicate on a non-medical triage set with fixed token cap; compare default vs RPD vs data-frame prompts.

claim: The RPD prompt gain is concentrated in under-called classes (self-care 13.4 to 29.8 percent; GPT-4.1 0 to 43.8) and does not help the already-strong non-emergency class (82.5 vs 82.0). It lowered accuracy in 13 of 45 vignettes (29 percent) and gave less consistent answers (modal share 76.9 to 66.9 percent).
schema_part: G1 (do not apply by schedule), S2
agent_test: Apply the prompt only on a signal (disagreement between attempts) and compare with always-on.

claim: Gains from a reasoning-strategy prompt shrink for reasoning-trained and newest models (o3 +4.4, GPT-4.1 mini +10.9; GPT-5.2 Instant -1.4). The paper reports a reasoning-model interaction OR 2.15 for RPD, which is about relative odds not absolute gain.
agent_test: Test strategy prompts on a strong vs weak model at equal tokens; report absolute gains.

claim: Extra explicit step-by-step reasoning can lower accuracy on tasks resting on implicit pattern learning or visual recognition (GPT-4o grammar 87.5 to 64.4; o1-preview 57.7 vs GPT-4o zero-shot 94.0; face recognition GPT-4o 64.0 to 51.2). Several models show no drop (Claude 3.5 Sonnet 65.9 vs 67.7). Verified in arXiv text this session. ToT 64.55 vs 62.52, still far below zero-shot. Same paper in b04/b05/c16-c18. Gema et al. 2025 add a second family: longer reasoning hurts on distractor, spurious-feature and constraint-tracking tasks (Claude Opus 4 to about 80 percent on Python distractors).
schema_part: G11 (think briefly; direct mode for pattern tasks)
agent_test: Add a no-reasoning direct arm on pattern-matching items and compare with S3 deliberation.
audit_note: ToT figures (64.55 vs 62.52) are on the 440-problem GPT-4o subset; otherwise all numbers match arXiv html of Liu et al. and Gema et al.

claim: Recognitional first options in human sport decisions are often at least as good as later ones: Johnson and Raab take-the-first (85 players, 31 trials) found first option better than later ones; replications are mixed (Belling 2014: option count not significant; Laborde and Raab 2013: experts fewer options than near-experts but not than non-experts; Klein and Peio chess: not significant).
agent_test: Vary candidate count 1,2,4 at equal tokens; check first-candidate quality vs later.

claim: Deliberate analysis is not uniformly better or worse under time pressure: unconscious thought meta-analysis d = 0.14 (CI -0.16 to 0.43) with expertise moderator opposite to theory; referees analytic 76.3 vs intuitive 74.7 percent (experts 84.3 vs novices 66.6).
agent_test: None direct; caution against claiming fast always beats slow.

claim: Scenario/decision-skill training with expert comparison (ShadowBox) improves human decision scoring: d = .63 (N=60), pre-post d = .38 (N=30, 10 got worse); video training for referees g = 1.718 (6 RCTs, N=163, I2 69.6 percent).
agent_test: Few-shot with expert-ranked exemplars vs none at equal tokens.

claim: Stress degrades human decision quality (police: training +3 points per level, service year -0.39, higher sympathetic arousal lower score); this is a human effect and transfer to an agent is unsupported.
agent_test: Not testable directly; token pressure is a different mechanism.

claim: RPD-enabled agent teams outperformed human-only teams in a command-and-control task (R-CAST: API 5.725 vs 4.748 at low switching; F=5.99, p=0.025; 10 vs 10 teams). Small student samples; same research group in 2005 and 2009.
agent_test: Compare RPD-structured agent vs plain agent in a multi-task switching benchmark.

claim: No study found that tests premortem, Critical Decision Method or data-frame sensemaking on LLMs beyond Kopka and Feufel; arXiv shows 1 RPD and 5 NDM results. LLM bias studies exist (o1 no bias in 7 of 10 vignette biases; CRT 96 percent GPT-4) but do not test NDM. Gap search added indirect tests only: always-on self-correction hurts (d06) and always-on verification helps fact precision (d11); trigger-only vs always-on still untested.
audit_note: arXiv search counts (1 RPD, 5 NDM) match; 7 of 10 no bias matches PMC; the CRT 96 percent for GPT-4 could not be seen on the abstract page (PDF unreadable) but is not central; the negative claim is bounded by 'found'.

claim: LLMs in an expert crisis simulation differ from 214 national-security experts on about half of actions without significance, are more aggressive on some measures, and are insensitive to persona; poor fidelity as expert stand-ins.
agent_test: Do not use LLM personas as expert proxies.

claim: On easy and familiar tasks the first solution is usually enough for reasoning models: first round correct in over 92 percent of cases using under 60 percent of tokens (QwQ, R1; math). Later rounds mostly repeat the same strategy. Removing redundant rounds cut tokens 48.6 percent on MATH500 with accuracy kept.
schema_part: S3/S4 take-the-first, G1 escalate only on failed check
agent_test: On a checkable set, compare first candidate vs best of 3 at equal tokens; report how often later candidates fix a first-candidate failure.

claim: Best use of extra test-time compute depends on difficulty: easy prompts gain from sequential revision, hard ones from a mix of sequential and parallel compute or from search; difficulty-matched allocation gives up to about 4x (2-4x) compute saving versus best-of-N on MATH with PaLM 2-S. At low token budgets skipping the think phase beats thinking at matched tokens (AMC23 51.3 vs 28.9 at 700 tokens) and parallel samples plus a verifier add more.
agent_test: Route by checkability and estimated difficulty; compare against always-deliberate at equal tokens. Models differ (distilled R1, PaLM 2-S, GPT-4o-mini), tasks are math.
audit_note: Snell et al. say easy questions favor sequential revisions while hard ones favor an ideal mix of sequential and parallel (or beam search against a PRM), and the 4x saving is an upper bound ('up to 4x', conclusion says 2-4x) on MATH with PaLM 2-S.
claim_before_audit: Best use of extra test-time compute depends on difficulty: easy prompts gain from sequential revision, hard ones from parallel sampling or search; difficulty-matched allocation saves about 4x compute versus best-of-N. At low token budgets skipping the think phase beats thinking at matched tokens (AMC23 51.3 vs 28.9 at 700 tokens) and parallel samples plus a verifier add more.

claim: Where an automatic verifier exists, many sampled candidates beat one careful candidate: coverage rises log-linearly with samples (SWE-bench Lite 15.9 to 56 percent with 250 samples). Without a verifier, vote and reward-model selection plateau.
agent_test: Use test-driven generate-and-test only where a cheap checker exists; otherwise vote.

claim: Intrinsic self-correction without an external signal does not help and can hurt older models (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after one round; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 after two). Oracle labels make it look good. This argues against an always-on critique or premortem pass.
schema_part: G1 trigger rules on external failed checks
agent_test: Compare critique-always vs critique-on-failed-check on a checkable set with current models, since 2023 results may not hold.

claim: More thinking tokens can hurt under noise: in distractor, spurious-feature and noisy-context tasks accuracy falls as reasoning grows (Claude Opus 4 to about 80 percent on Python distractors; NoisyBench drops up to 80 percent). Prompting alone did not fix noisy context; few-shot examples fixed the spurious-feature regression failure. Token caps shrink length with small loss (TALE: 67 percent fewer tokens, under 3 percent accuracy loss) but too small a cap hurts.
agent_test: Test cap vs no cap on distractor-heavy items; findings are model-specific and tasks were built to expose the effect.
